hook.en: Antarctica was once part of a warm supercontinent with rich plant and animal life. How do we know, and why does it matter?

objectives.en: Explain why Antarctica holds clues to the earth's past

narration.en: Antarctica was once part of a warm supercontinent with rich plant and animal life. How do we know, and why does it matter?

body.en: About 650 million years ago, a giant southern supercontinent called Gondwana existed, centred roughly around present-day Antarctica. The climate was much warmer and it supported a huge variety of plants and animals. After the dinosaurs were wiped out and the age of mammals began, the landmass broke apart into the continents and countries we know.

points.en: Warmer, full of life; later split apart

say.en: About 650 million years ago, Gondwana existed in the south.
It was warm and full of plants and animals.

text.en: Warm climate, rich plants and animals

say.en: After the dinosaurs vanished, the age of mammals began.
The landmass broke up into continents and countries.
Today Antarctica's ice keeps records of the ancient atmosphere.

text.en: Today: ice holds ancient carbon records

body.en: Antarctica holds about 90 per cent of the earth's total ice. Its layers of ice have trapped air and carbon from hundreds of thousands of years ago, so scientists study it to understand the planet's past, present and possible future. Visiting it helps us see where we have come from and where we may be heading.

problem.en: Why is Antarctica a good place to understand the earth's past?

steps.en: It was the centre of the old supercontinent Gondwana.
Its layers of ice trap ancient air and carbon.
Scientists read these layers like a record book.

answer.en: Antarctica lay at the heart of Gondwana, and its thick ice has trapped air and carbon from hundreds of thousands of years ago. Scientists read these layers like a record, learning how the earth's climate has changed over time.
